summary:
A trans visitor to Vermont remains subject in full to the United States federal travel framework. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020). The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments have responded: in April 2025 CNN reported that several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US.

Within Vermont itself, the state stands as one of the more protective jurisdictions on gender-identity nondiscrimination as of July 2026, though the federal layer, including the DC House bathroom ban, means that tier on its own can no longer be considered most protective. Vermont has shield laws enacted in 2023 and 2024 that are enforceable against out-of-state action, placing it among the states with such protections.

Facilities access is restricted in a growing number of states. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

State document rules are tightening elsewhere. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences and invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Visa screening carries its own exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the US to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication, and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported being denied care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes, with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained for visitors needing it. Executive Order 14187 (January 2025) described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

outOfScopeNotes:
The July 2026 national risk assessment's specific criteria for its "Do Not Travel" state designations, and whether Vermont's protective status affects any federal screening or document outcome for a visitor, are not resolved in the sources reviewed here.

The scope of Vermont's 2023 and 2024 shield laws, including which specific forms of care or legal proceedings they cover and how they interact with federal subpoenas such as the summer 2025 Department of Justice hospital records demand, is not fully detailed in the inventory.

Whether Vermont's nondiscrimination protections alter TSA screening procedures, passport processing, or visa adjudication for a visitor physically present in the state is not addressed by the sources; those processes are federal.

The outcomes of the ACLU's suit against the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and of challenges to the federal care restrictions that have been blocked or enjoined, remain unresolved in the sources reviewed here.
